"Love me, love me not"

I am trying to wrap my head around the new proposed Russian sanctions.

US relaxed Russian sanctions so that oil prices don't go crazy during the height of the crisis and allow India to be feasible.

India basically mopped up whatever Russian crude they could in the past 5 months, even after the sanctions waiver expired on 17 June.

China joined the party as well. We also have Indonesia that signed up for 150 mb of Russian crude to bolster national energy security.

So if the sanctions are back, does US expect these countries to stop buying Russian due to the additional tariffs of up to 100%, and go back to Middle Eastern crude of which there is a shortfall of 10 mbd without recovery of flows at the Strait of Hormuz & Bab el-Mandeb? 

Or do they just want refined products to go crazy next because these refineries won't have enough crude to run?

(The waiver on the Iranian sanctions during the crisis also make me think it was a "Love me, love me not" scenario, but that's another story).

Crude oil prices have fallen as Iran and the United States de-escalate their fighting and intensify indirect talks via Oman and other intermediaries to re-open the Strait of Hormuz.

Hedge funds and other money managers sold the equivalent of 28 million barrels in the six most important petroleum futures and options contracts over the seven days ending on August 4.

Fund sales were the first in four weeks and came after managers had purchased a total of 193 million barrels since July 7 as the previous ceasefire broke down ...

#Agriculture: Global food prices rose to a three-year high last month as summer heatwaves and conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East lifted crop costs, potentially feeding through to higher consumer prices in the coming months. The UN FAO Food Price Index reached its highest since January 2023, although the year-on-year increase remained contained at just 1%. Sugar led the monthly rise at 5.6%, followed by grains at 3.4% and vegetable oils at 2%, while meat fell 2.8% and dairy declined 0.7%.

COT on #commodities covering managed money activity in the week to 4 August, a period that saw the BCOM Index fall 1.2% as weakness across energy and grains was only partly offset by strength in precious and industrial metals, as well as softs.

Crude oil: Renewed price weakness drove a 25k reduction in the combined crude net long to 266k contracts, following 171k of net buying during the previous three weeks. Meanwhile, the natural gas net short reached a 27-month high at 89k contracts as prices remained under pressure, with ample supply keeping inventories well above seasonal averages.

Metals: Ahead of Wednesday’s technical upside break, managed money accounts had already increased their gold net long to a January high of 132k contracts. The increase was driven in part by short covering, with gross shorts slashed by 42% to a 19-month low of just 9.4k contracts. The silver net long jumped 32%, while platinum traders lifted their net long by 71%.

Meanwhile, a 4.5% rally in copper during the reporting week, which extended to a record high last Thursday, helped lift the net long to a 5½-year high of 77.8k contracts.

Grains: Except for corn, the sector saw broad selling, although the combined 73k net reduction was relatively modest compared with the 542k contracts speculators had added during the previous five weeks.

Elsewhere: The cotton net long reached a 16-month high, while six consecutive weeks of net selling cut the live cattle net long to a 22-month low.
